newsitem.title: FINLAND: INTERVIEW-Finnish PK Cables targets telecom growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Finnish PK Cables targets telecom growth.

text.p: Finnish electric wiring and components maker PK Cables Oy sees its main growth potential in supplying the telecommunications industry, the group's chief executive said on Tuesday.

"It's clear that telecommunications, the world's fastest growing industry, is the area where we too expect the strongest growth," PK Cables CEO Tom Hakalax told Reuters by telephone after the company said it planned an initial public offering.
"We have almost 30 years of experience in the automotive industry, and we have found our own narrow segment of expertise," Hakalax said.

PK produces, mainly for export, cable harnesses (72 percent of 1996 net sales) for the vehicle, telecom and household appliance industries, as well as line cords (11 percent), and assembles mobile telephone base stations (17 percent).
Net sales were 260 million markka in 1996, up from 183 million in 1995 with profit before extras up 27 percent to 37 million. For 1996 it paid a dividend of one markka per share.
In telecommunications, its main product is mobile phone base stations which it assembles under subcontract to Finnish telcoms major Nokia Oy, Hakalax said.
"Our special competence is in logistics and management of material flows and, of course, in assembly technology and processing," he said.
The group's high-skill operations are based in Finland with subcontracted manufacturing in low-cost Russia and Estonia.
Its biggest profit margins are in its traditional area, making cable harnesses for the automotive industry.
"Our traditional product is very labour-intensive ... and that generates a great deal of value-added," Hakalax said.
"The margins (on PK Cables' telecommunications business) are clearly lower than in our traditional business, but the revenues are considerable because of the volumes," he said.
The company in its present form was created in 1994 when institutional shareholders and management shareholders bought the operations of former units of what today is Nokia.
Its institutional investors are mainly private equity funds managed by venture capital company CapMan Capital Management Oy and Harju Elekter AS.
"All in all, the company's earnings and profitability are expected to remain good in the 1997 financial year," it said in a statement with its share issue announcement.
It said net sales of wiring harnesses for the truck industry are expected to grow significantly in 1997 with good delivery prospects and partly thanks to new products.
Its long-term objective is to dampen fluctuations in the business cycles in Europe by starting up production in Brazil.
"We intend to start production there in in the second half of this year," Hakalax said, adding that the group had already found suitable production facilities to lease.
Once it is up and running in about a year from now, the Brazil operation would initially have net sales of about 40 million markka and about 40 to 50 employees, he said.
